content: The Cartesian coordinate system, also known as the rectangular coordinate system, is a mathematical framework used to uniquely identify points in a plane or space using numerical values. In two dimensions, each point is defined by an ordered pair of numbers, typically referred to as the x-coordinate (abscissa) and the y-coordinate (ordinate). These coordinates are determined by two perpendicular axes, the x-axis and the y-axis, which intersect at a point called the origin. A unit length is chosen and marked along these axes to create a grid. For example, a circle with a radius of 2 can be represented algebraically by the equation (x^2 + y^2 = 4). The system is named after René Descartes, a French mathematician and philosopher who introduced the concept in 1637. Descartes' work merged algebra with Euclidean geometry, laying the foundation for analytic geometry and influencing fields such as calculus and cartography. In his writings, Descartes described how to specify the position of a point on a surface using two intersecting axes as reference lines. In a two-dimensional Cartesian coordinate system, the horizontal axis is labeled as the x-axis, and the vertical axis is labeled as the y-axis. Together, these axes form a plane known as the xy-plane. The intersection of the axes, the origin, is denoted as (O). Points in this system are specified using ordered pairs ((x, y)), where the x-coordinate is listed first, followed by the y-coordinate. The plane is divided into four regions, called quadrants, which are labeled counterclockwise starting from the upper right quadrant. In the first quadrant, both coordinates are positive; in the second quadrant, the x-coordinate is negative and the y-coordinate is positive; in the third quadrant, both coordinates are negative; and in the fourth quadrant, the x-coordinate is positive and the y-coordinate is negative. In three dimensions, the Cartesian coordinate system extends to include a third axis, the z-axis, which is perpendicular to both the xand y-axes. This system allows for the representation of three-dimensional space, with points specified by ordered triples ((x, y, z)). The z-axis typically represents height, while the xand y-axes represent length and width, respectively. The three axes divide space into eight regions, called octants, analogous to the quadrants in two dimensions. The first octant contains points where all three coordinates are positive. The orientation of the axes in three dimensions can be described as either right-handed or left-handed, depending on the direction of the z-axis relative to the xand y-axes. The right-hand rule is commonly used to determine the positive orientation of the axes. The orientation of the axes in two dimensions is determined by the choice of the positive direction for the y-axis, given a fixed x-axis. The standard orientation, known as the right-handed orientation, has the positive x-axis pointing to the right and the positive y-axis pointing upward. This orientation can be visualized using the right-hand rule, where the thumb points upward and the fingers curl from the x-axis to the y-axis. Reversing the roles of the xand y-axes or using the left-hand rule results in a left-handed orientation. In three dimensions, the orientation of the z-axis is determined once the xand y-axes are fixed. The right-handed system is the standard orientation, where the z-axis points upward, and the xand y-axes form a positively oriented plane. The right-hand rule can also be applied here: the thumb, index finger, and middle finger of the right hand point in the directions of the x-, y-, and z-axes, respectively. Conversely, using the left hand results in a left-handed system. Different disciplines may use different conventions; for example, mathematicians often use a right-handed system, while engineers may use a left-handed system, which can lead to confusion in interdisciplinary work. A point in a Cartesian coordinate system can also be represented as a vector, which is an arrow pointing from the origin to the point. In three dimensions, this vector can be expressed as (mathbf{r} = xmathbf{i} + ymathbf{j} + zmathbf{k}), where (mathbf{i}), (mathbf{j}), and (mathbf{k}) are unit vectors along the x-, y-, and z-axes, respectively. These unit vectors are known as the versors of the coordinate system and form the standard basis in three-dimensional space. The Cartesian coordinate system is widely used in various fields to represent spatial dimensions and other quantities, such as time, mass, or force. The system can also be extended to higher dimensions, allowing for the representation of relationships between more than three variables. Although higher-dimensional spaces are difficult to visualize, the algebraic principles of Cartesian coordinates can be applied to perform calculations involving multiple variables. In computational geometry, the Cartesian coordinate system serves as the foundation for the algebraic manipulation of geometric shapes. Other coordinate systems, such as polar or spherical coordinates, have been developed for specific applications. It is speculated that the use of grids by Renaissance artists to break down their subjects may have influenced Descartes' development of the Cartesian system, although this remains conjectural.
